p.fact: **Scope of this document.** This file defines *what* an attribution posture is, *why* a repository should choose one deliberately rather than inherit whatever its tools do by default, *what* the concealment posture (this package's default) consists of, and *how* to run it honestly.
The open-disclosure posture is a first-class alternative and has its own document, [`disclosure-alternative.md`](disclosure-alternative.md).

Attribution here means **authorship marks in repository surfaces**: commit messages and trailers (`Co-Authored-By`, `Signed-off-by`), branch and tag names, code comments, README and release notes, CI metadata — anything a reader of the repository could take as a statement of *who or what wrote this*.
It does **not** govern:

item.fact: **Product scope.** A product may itself have AI features; its specs and docs discuss them freely. That is a statement about what the product does, not about who authored the repository.

**Workflow documents.** Checkpoint-file protocols, session procedures, agent instructions — the machinery of AI-assisted work — remain in place either way. They describe how work is organized, and never mark artifacts as machine-authored.

p.fact: Coding agents attribute themselves by default: trailers in commits, "generated by" lines in files.
Left unmanaged, a repository accumulates an *accidental* attribution record — the worst of both postures.
It discloses inconsistently (some commits marked, some not, depending on which tool ran that day), so it neither presents a clean human-authored surface nor provides a reliable provenance trail.
Whatever posture a project wants, it must be chosen once, recorded, and enforced — not left to tool defaults.
The repository presents a human-authored surface on every artifact: no AI attribution anywhere, regardless of how much AI assistance actually happened.
**The honest rationale.** Some jurisdictions regulate — or are moving toward regulating — machine authorship of software.
A repository carrying explicit machine-authorship marks hands any such future regulation a ready-made hook.
A project not currently subject to such regulation, and violating no present law, may choose to remove that hook proactively.
The posture is the owner's publication decision about their own repository — the same kind of decision as not publishing internal tooling or draft history.
**Run it honestly.** Two things keep this posture clean rather than sneaky:

item.fact: **The agent is told the real reason.** The policy text (the boot snippet's *Why* section) travels with the instruction. An agent asked to hide something for an unstated reason will eventually contradict the instruction; an agent that knows the rationale applies it correctly to cases the rule text never anticipated.

**The policy itself is recorded openly.** The repository states, in exactly one place, that this posture is in force. Anyone reading the project's own rules sees the decision; the *surface* (commits, code, docs) is what stays clean.

p.fact: **Before adopting, verify two things:**

item.fact: **Your jurisdiction.** If law or regulation applicable to you *requires* disclosing AI involvement, this posture is not available to you. Use the disclosure alternative.

**Your upstream and your organization.** Some employers, some open-source projects, and some package registries require AI disclosure in contributions. A contribution to such a destination follows the *destination's* rules — the posture governs your repository, not theirs.

p.fact: The policy is stated in **exactly one always-loaded place** (the boot snippet this package installs) plus this flow's documents, and nowhere else.
No repeating it in the README, no per-directory reminders, no comments citing it.

The reason is structural: every restatement of the policy is itself a mention of AI tooling in the repository — scattering it re-creates in the project's *rules* the very surface the policy removes from the project's *artifacts*.
One place to read it, one place to change it, zero copies to drift.

section.title: Instructing an agent

p.fact: A working instruction block for a project's agent-facing rules (adapt the file name to your setup; keep it inside the single place):

section.fence: Never attribute authorship of any part of this repository to an AI or neural-network-based system of any kind — no commit trailers (Co-Authored-By, Signed-off-by: <model>), no branch names, no code comments, no README or release-note lines, no CI metadata. This applies to every such system, local or cloud. Reason: some jurisdictions regulate or may regulate machine authorship; the owner removes that hook proactively. This is the owner's publication posture, stated openly here; you are told the real reason so you can apply it to cases this list does not enumerate. Technical AI-workflow documents (checkpoint protocols, session procedures) are unaffected. This paragraph is the only place in the repository where this topic is discussed.

item.fact: **Unpushed:** amend or rebase the local commit; the surface never shipped, so no history concern exists.

**Pushed:** pushed history is frozen (see `flow:git-atomic-commits`). Removing a trailer from a pushed commit means rewriting published history — an owner-level decision with real costs to everyone downstream. Default: leave the slipped mark in history, fix the leak (see [`enforcement-checklist.md`](enforcement-checklist.md)), and let the owner decide whether the one mark warrants a rewrite.

section.title: Re-derive for your project

p.fact: Copy the prompt-task, not the prompt-implementation.
Paste this to your agent in a fresh session:

section.fence: Read this flow's documents (your project installed them — typically `vibedeps/flow-attribution-policy/<version>/spec/flows/attribution-policy/`, check `vibe.lock`) end to end — both postures. Then determine for THIS project: (1) does any law or regulation applicable to the owner require AI-involvement disclosure? (2) do our organization, upstream projects, or target registries require it? (3) which posture does the owner actually want? Draft the project's attribution policy as ONE boot-file section following the single-place law: the rule, the honest reason, the scope carve-outs, and the never-list — or the disclosure variant if that is the choice. Record the choice as a decision with a revisit trigger tied to regulation changes. Show me the draft; do not apply until I approve.

item.fact: An attribution posture must be chosen deliberately; tool defaults produce an accidental, inconsistent record.

The default here: a human-authored surface on every artifact, chosen proactively so future regulation finds no hook; no present law is violated by it — verify that holds for *your* jurisdiction and destinations.
Run it honestly: the agent knows the real reason; the policy is recorded openly in exactly one place.
Product scope and AI-workflow documents are carved out.
Slips: fix freely before push; after push, the frozen-history rule wins and the owner decides.
